content: Toward the end of the 19th century, scientists began to recognize the significant role that ticks could play as vectors for transmitting diseases. By the late 20th century, several tick-borne diseases, including babesiosis, Lyme disease, and ehrlichiosis, were identified in the United States. Ehrlichiosis is caused by various bacterial species belonging to the genus Ehrlichia (pronounced err-lick-ee-uh), which were first recognized in 1935. Over the years, veterinary pathogens from this genus were found to cause diseases in animals such as dogs, cattle, sheep, goats, and horses. Currently, three species of Ehrlichia in the United States and one in Japan are known to cause disease in humans, with the possibility of additional species being identified as diagnostic methods improve. The first Ehrlichia species known to infect humans was identified in Japan in 1953. This pathogen, Ehrlichia sennetsu, causes Sennetsu fever, a condition characterized by fever and swollen lymph nodes. Sennetsu fever is extremely rare outside of the Far East and Southeast Asia, with most cases reported in western Japan. In the United States, human diseases caused by Ehrlichia species have been recognized since the mid-1980s. These diseases, collectively referred to as ehrlichioses, are clinically similar but differ in their epidemiology and causative agents. The primary species responsible for human ehrlichiosis in the U.S. are Ehrlichia chaffeensis, Ehrlichia ewingii, and a bacterium closely related or identical to Ehrlichia phagocytophila. Human ehrlichiosis caused by Ehrlichia chaffeensis was first described in 1987. This disease primarily occurs in the southeastern and south-central regions of the United States and is transmitted by the lone star tick (Amblyomma americanum). Human granulocytic ehrlichiosis (HGE), the second recognized ehrlichial infection in humans in the U.S., was first described in 1994. The causative species of HGE has not been formally named but is closely related or identical to the veterinary pathogens Ehrlichia equi and Ehrlichia phagocytophila. HGE is transmitted by the blacklegged tick (Ixodes scapularis) and the western blacklegged tick (Ixodes pacificus). The most recently identified human pathogen, Ehrlichia ewingii, has caused disease in a limited number of patients, primarily in Missouri, Oklahoma, and Tennessee. Most of these patients had underlying immunosuppressive conditions. The full geographic range, vectors, and role of Ehrlichia ewingii in human disease are still under investigation. The initial symptoms of ehrlichiosis can resemble nonspecific signs and symptoms seen in other infectious or non-infectious diseases. It is not clear whether all individuals infected with Ehrlichia bacteria develop symptoms. Some individuals may experience a mild illness that does not prompt them to seek medical attention, while others may remain entirely asymptomatic. The diagnosis of ehrlichiosis relies on a combination of clinical signs, symptoms, and confirmatory laboratory tests. Blood samples can be sent to specialized reference laboratories for testing, although the availability of specific diagnostic tests varies. Laboratory findings that may suggest ehrlichiosis include a low white blood cell count, a low platelet count, and elevated liver enzyme levels. When ehrlichiosis is strongly suspected based on clinical and epidemiological findings, appropriate antibiotic treatment should be initiated immediately. Treatment should not be delayed while awaiting laboratory confirmation. Fever typically resolves within 24 to 72 hours after starting treatment with doxycycline or other tetracycline antibiotics. A lack of rapid response to tetracycline therapy may indicate an alternative diagnosis. Preventative antibiotic treatment is not recommended for individuals who are asymptomatic but have recently been bitten by a tick. Transmission of Ehrlichia bacteria from ticks to humans may require several hours of tick attachment, so early removal of ticks can significantly reduce the risk of infection.
